challenges.name: redis-data-structures-quiz
challenges.title: Choose the structure by access pattern
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the contest-night leaderboard incident: the shipped write path with the size of its key, and a MONITOR capture of two API instances updating scores at the same moment.

questions.explanation: False. The hash fixes the write path: HINCRBY changes one field on the server, sends a few bytes and cannot lose a concurrent update. But a hash has no order. Redis cannot return "the ten largest fields" of a hash, so the top-10 endpoint would still need HGETALL (all 40,000 fields) and a sort in Node.js on every request. The structure whose cheap operations include both "add points to one member" and "read the top N" is a sorted set: ZINCRBY and ZRANGE ... REV (or ZREVRANGE), O(log N) plus the ten members returned. The misconception is that splitting a big string into fields solves every access pattern; it solves the ones that touch a single field.

questions.question:
redis-cli MONITOR on the primary during the contest (two API instances, 10.0.1.5 and 10.0.1.6; values shortened):

1792004400.101 [0 10.0.1.5:51234] "GET" "leaderboard:global"
1792004400.103 [0 10.0.1.6:40022] "GET" "leaderboard:global"
1792004400.140 [0 10.0.1.5:51234] "SET" "leaderboard:global" "{...\"u_88\":430,\"u_91\":120...}"
1792004400.142 [0 10.0.1.6:40022] "SET" "leaderboard:global" "{...\"u_88\":400,\"u_91\":150...}"

Both SET commands replied OK.

Statement: "After these four commands, the +30 points that instance 10.0.1.5 added for u_88 are no longer in Redis."
questions.explanation: True. Both instances read the same version of the string (u_88 = 400). Instance .5 wrote 430 for u_88; instance .6, which had read the old version, then wrote its own copy with u_88 = 400 and u_91 = 150, replacing the whole value. Both writes succeeded, and one update is gone. Redis executes each command atomically, but a GET followed by a SET from one client is not atomic: other clients' commands run in between. ZINCRBY (or HINCRBY) performs the read-modify-write inside one command, and MULTI/EXEC with WATCH or a Lua script can make several commands act as one. The misconception is that because Redis is single-threaded, application code that reads and then writes is safe.
